 AN CHÚIRT UACHTARACH 

 THE SUPREME COURT 

 S:AP:IE:2025:000048 

 [2026] IESC 1 

 Dunne J. 

 Woulfe J. 

 Hogan J. 

 Collins J. 

 Donnelly J. 

   

 BETWEEN 

 PROTECT EAST MEATH LIMITED 

 Applicant/Appellant 

 AND 

 MEATH COUNTY COUNCIL 

 Respondent 

   

 

 JUDGMENT of Mr. Justice Maurice Collins delivered on 22 January 2026 

 

 1.                          Mandamus is a discretionary remedy: Brady v Cavan County Council [1999] IESC 49 , [1999] 4 IR 99 (" Brady "), per Keane J (as he then was) at 103; Murphy J (dissenting but not on this issue) at 124. Mandamus will not - at least in general - issue to compel a public body to perform a statutory duty if compliance with such an order would be impossible. But quite apart from any question of impossibility - and any rule that mandamus will not issue where compliance is impossible requires significant qualification, at least where such impossibility arises solely from resource constraints - a court has a discretion to decline to grant an order of mandamus , even in the face of a proven or (as here) admitted breach of statutory duty. It is necessary in every case to undertake a broader assessment than merely asking whether compliance is strictly impossible: as Murray J explained in Re McD (A Child) [2024] IESC 6 , [2024] 2 ILRM 153: 

 "everything depends on the nature of the duty, the interests of the applicant for the relief in play, the impact upon the applicant if the relief they seek is not granted, the period of time over which the public body has been [in] default, the type of public body in issue (and in particular how it is financed), the reason the public body gives for not complying with the duty, and the consequence in a particular case of the court granting such mandatory relief" (§13). 

 As Hogan J put it in his judgment in Re McD (A Child) , an order of mandamus will " only be made where it is just and convenient to do so " and that " will in turn depend on the statutory context " (§93). 

 2.                          In making that assessment, a plea of lack of resources on the part of the public body concerned will not necessarily be given decisive weight. Where the Oireachtas legislates to impose statutory duties on a public body - at least where, as here, such duties are imposed in unqualified terms - citizens may reasonably expect that the resources necessary to enable those duties to be performed adequately will be made available to the public body concerned (or, alternatively, that the public body will be empowered to raise the necessary resources directly). The enactment of legislation should not be seen as a performative activity or, in the vivid language of Hogan J in B (A Minor) v Child and Family Agency [2025] IESC 2, " a form of legislative Potemkin village " (§64). As the UK Supreme Court (per Lord Sales) rightly observed in R (Imam) v Croydon London Borough Council [2023] UKSC 45 , [2025] AC 335 , if courts routinely decline to compel public bodies to perform their statutory duties on the grounds of absence of sufficient resources, that effectively qualifies and dilutes the duty that has been imposed by law and undermines the rule of law and the separation of powers: §40. 

   

 3.                          Lord Sales' analysis applies with at least equal force in our Constitutional order. Even so, as the decision in R (Imam) v Croydon London Borough Council itself illustrates, a court must in every case carefully consider all the circumstances and assess ( inter alia ) the impact of making an order of mandamus on the public body, as well as the impact of denying such an order, both in terms of the direct impact on the applicant and the less direct (but nonetheless potentially significant) impact on the rule of law and respect for it. Orders of mandamus should neither be made, nor refused, routinely or as a matter of course or on the basis of any default rule. But upholding the rule of law and giving life and force to the statutory duties that the Oireachtas has considered it appropriate to impose on public bodies, must always be a very weighty consideration. 

   

   

 4.                          That Irish law does not necessarily attribute decisive weight to a plea of lack of resources in this context is demonstrated in concrete terms by this Court's decisions in Re McD (A Child) and B (A Minor) v Child and Family Agency . The statutory regime at issue in those appeals was, of course, very different to that with which Brady was concerned, as was emphasised in the judgments given in both appeals. But that in itself serves to make the fundamental point that lack of resources is not to be regarded as a sort of universal wild card that, once played, excludes the making of a mandatory order.   

   

 5.                          It is, perhaps, easy to overlook the fact that the actual order sought by the applicants in Brady - which was limited to the repair of a specific roadway in the vicinity of the applicants' respective residences - was one which the respondent county council had the resources to implement. Brady was not, therefore, a case of true impossibility and is perhaps best understood as one in which the real concern of the Court was that an order of mandamus would disrupt the road repair programme which had been adopted by the council in order to achieve compliance with its statutory duties. Even so, the majority's analysis is notable for its somewhat one-eyed conception of the proper role of the separation of powers in this context. So far from respecting the separation of powers, if the courts were to routinely acquiesce in a situation in which the Oireachtas has solemnly legislated to impose statutory duties and obligations on public bodies in the public interest, but where lack of resources deprives those duties and obligations of any concrete reality, that would wholly undermine the separation of powers  and the rule of law. Laws enacted by the Oireachtas must be given effect by the Executive (and by the courts) unless and until amended by the Oireachtas . That is the key lesson from Re McD (A Child) and B (A Minor) v Child and Family Agency . 

 6.                        Here, Meath County Council was in long term default in respect of the statutory duty imposed by section 19(1) of the Planning and Development Act 2000 (" the 2000 Act ") (now repealed). That duty was expressed in clear and unqualified terms. Local area plans (LAPs) are (or, at any events, were) a significant element of the architecture of the 2000 Act and the absence of an operative LAP for the East Meath area is potentially significant for development in that area. No satisfactory explanation for the Council's failure to comply with its section 19(1) duty (which failure is not confined to the East Meath LAP area) has been given and - strikingly - no proposals to remedy its default were made by the Council until the eve of the hearing of the appeal by this Court. There is no suggestion that the Council's default arose from any lack of financial resources. Insofar as a lack of personnel resources is relied on, the Council's evidence was very limited, and the solution belatedly proposed - the engagement of third-party contractors to assist in the preparation of the relevant LAP(s) - was in any event one that was always available to the Council. In reality, the Council appears to have taken the view that compliance with section 19(1) was not a priority and that it would in any event be relieved of that duty on the commencement of Part 3 of the Planning and Development Act 2024 (" the 2024 Act "). As was the case in Re McD (A Child) , it is difficult to avoid the impression that the Council took it upon itself " to disregard that which the Oireachtas has prescribed as mandatory " (per Hogan J at §97). As a public body bound by law, it was not entitled to take such an approach. 

 7.                        Having regard to these considerations, I agree with Woulfe J that it would, in principle, be appropriate to make an order of mandamus in this case and that the High Court erred in declining to do so. The Council did not identify any basis on which its failure to adopt an East Meath LAP in accordance with section 19(1) of the 2000 Act should be excused, nor has it shown that the making of an order of mandamus directing it to comply with its section 19(1) duty now would of itself impose an inappropriate burden on it and/or impact unduly on its capacity to discharge its other statutory duties and functions. 

 8.                        However, subsequent to the hearing of this appeal the Court was told that the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage had made an Order commencing Chapters 5 and 6 of Part 3 of the 2024 Act with effect from 31 December 2025 and repealing the provisions of Part 2, Chapter 2 of the 2000 Act (dealing with LAPs) with effect from the same date. [1] The making of that Order, and in particular the repeal of Part 2, Chapter 2 of the 2000 Act, may impact on the issue of whether it is appropriate to make an order of mandamus against the Council at this point in time. I agree that the parties should be heard as to the orders to be made in light of this development. 

   

   

   

 [1] Planning and Development Act 2024 (Commencement) (No 5) Order 2025 (SI No 633 of 2025).
